Round three: the dragon wins initiative, bites, and hits the second 8th-level fighter for 23 hit points. The two fighters strike; one hits, for another 10 hit points of subdual. The chance is now 77:88 (7/8), or 87.5% (treat as 88%). The referee rolls 89.

Length of subdual: a dragon stays subdued for an indefinite time. But if it is not strongly held, well treated, given plenty of treasure, and allowed ample freedom, it will try to kill its captor and/or escape. Evil dragons never serve a good master for long, and good dragons are 50% more likely to kill or escape from a neutral captor than from one of their own alignment. Several dragons: two dragons met outside their lair are a mated pair; three or more are sub-adults. Two or more met in their lair are a mated pair, with their young if any. Mated pairs are always of the 5th through 8th ages. Young in the lair are eggs (10%) or very young (90%). If the young are attacked, both adults automatically breathe and then close to bite, with a ferocity bonus of +2 to hit and +1/+3 to clawing/biting damage. If either of a mated pair is attacked, the other rushes to defend it with the same ferocity bonuses, unless it is attacked at the same time.

Treasure: very young dragons usually have none, with a 10% chance of one-quarter the listed treasure. Young dragons have a 25% chance of one-quarter the listed treasure, and sub-adults a 50% chance of one-half. Young adults and old dragons have normal treasure. Very old and ancient dragons are 50% and 75% likely to have 150% and 200% of the listed treasure, respectively.

Weaknesses: the innate cowardice of dragonkind shows in the fact that most can be subdued. Their egotism makes them open to flattery, and leads the more stupid ones to attack other powerful creatures they see as challenging their dominance. Greed and avarice drive all but the loftiest dragons (40% of silver, 80% of gold, and the platinum dragon), so very clever persons can manipulate them, as can the sight of real treasure and the promise of more.

Saving throws: once a dragon has 5 or more hit points per die, it saves as if its hit dice were its total hit points divided by 4, which is higher than its actual number. This reflects its magic resistance and general toughness. On the other hand, even a very young dragon, with only 1 hit point per die, saves according to its actual number of hit dice, for the same reason.

  4. Creatures with 6 or more hit dice automatically ignore the aura.
  5. The aura of adult, old, and very old dragons is weaker than an ancient dragon’s, so saves against it are at +5, +3, and +1 respectively. system.description:
Chance of: speaking 100%; magic use 100%; sleeping 5%.

Bahamut the platinum dragon, King of the Good dragons, lives in a great fortified palace behind the east wind. (No one but Bahamut and his court knows for certain whether it is on the elemental plane of air or on some plane between it and the Seven Heavens or Tri-Paradises.) About one-quarter of the time he roams the earth as a human or almost any other form he likes, since he can shape change freely. He can travel astrally or ethereally.

  • Attacks: two claws and a bite, or one of three breath weapons, each usable twice per day. All saving throws against his breath are at −3 because of its power.
  • Cold: a cone 8” long with a 3” base.
  • Vapor: a cloud that makes those inside save versus dragon breath or lose their substance and take gaseous form for 12 full turns.
  • Sonic vibration: disintegrates up to 150 hit points.
  • Spells: any of 1st through 7th level: two magic-user and one cleric spell of each level per day, a maximum of 21 spells. He has books listing every known magic-user spell of these levels.
  • Guards: seven huge ancient gold dragons of the highest ability and loyalty serve as his guards, companions, and advisors, and he is seldom (10%) without them.

(A sage tells of meeting Bahamut disguised as an old hermit, with seven canaries singing sweetly as they flitted nearby. He says he would never have known the hermit was anything but what he seemed, except that a group of ogres and trolls happened by, much to their sorrow . . .)

Length of subdual: a dragon stays subdued for an indefinite time. But if it is not strongly held, well treated, given plenty of treasure, and allowed ample freedom, it will try to kill its captor and/or escape. The older and more powerful the dragon, the less likely it is to stay subdued, and an intelligent, spell-using dragon is unlikely to stay subdued at all; it is more likely to try to take over its captor and rule his holdings. Evil dragons never serve a good master for long, and good dragons are 50% more likely to kill or escape from a neutral captor than from one of their own alignment. Players may sell or give a dragon to another player, or keep it in their own service. A dragon cannot be subdued again unless it has actually regained its freedom.

Several dragons: two dragons met outside their lair are a mated pair; three or more are sub-adults. Two or more met in their lair are a mated pair, with their young if any. Mated pairs are always of the 5th through 8th ages. Young in the lair are eggs (10%) or very young (90%). If the young are attacked, both adults automatically breathe and then close to bite, with a ferocity bonus of +2 to hit and +1/+3 to clawing/biting damage. If either of a mated pair is attacked, the other rushes to defend it with the same ferocity bonuses, unless it is attacked at the same time.

Treasure: very young dragons usually have none, with a 10% chance of one-quarter the listed treasure. Young dragons have a 25% chance of one-quarter the listed treasure, and sub-adults a 50% chance of one-half. Young adults and old dragons have normal treasure. Very old and ancient dragons are 50% and 75% likely to have 150% and 200% of the listed treasure, respectively.

Weaknesses: the innate cowardice of dragonkind shows in the fact that most can be subdued. Their egotism makes them open to flattery, and leads the more stupid ones to attack other powerful creatures they see as challenging their dominance. Greed and avarice drive all but the loftiest dragons (40% of silver, 80% of gold, and the platinum dragon), so very clever persons can manipulate them, as can the sight of real treasure and the promise of more.

Saving throws: once a dragon has 5 or more hit points per die, it saves as if its hit dice were its total hit points divided by 4, which is higher than its actual number. This reflects its magic resistance and general toughness. On the other hand, even a very young dragon, with only 1 hit point per die, saves according to its actual number of hit dice, for the same reason.
system.hpNote: Size (d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge) sets the hit dice; age (d8) sets the hit points per die (MM p.29).

Silver dragons make their homes on mountain peaks, in clouds, and similar places. They are said to be found in the home of the King of Good Dragons, and behind other winds as well.   • Spells: a magic-using silver dragon can use at most ten spells. At each of its first two ages it gains two spells (1st level at the first, 2nd level at the second). At each age after that it gains one more: 3rd level at sub-adult and young adult, 4th level at adult and old, and 5th level at very old and ancient. So a very young one knows two 1st-level spells, a young one two 1st- and two 2nd-level spells, etc.

Size: each of the ten species comes in three sizes (small, average, and huge). Roll d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge. Size sets the dragon’s number of hit dice.

Age: dragons pass through eight ages. Roll d8 for the age, which sets the hit points per die:

d8AgeYearsHit points per die
1Very young1-51
2Young6-152
3Sub-adult16-253
4Young adult26-504
5Adult51-1005
6Old101-2006
7Very old201-4007
8Ancient401+8

Senses: all dragons see equally well by day or in darkness (infravision, 60’), and have excellent sight, smell, and hearing. These keen senses let them detect hidden or invisible creatures within 1” per age level.

Fear aura: from adult age onward, a dragon flying overhead or charging radiates a powerful aura that causes fear:

  1. All creatures under 1 hit die, and any non-carnivorous creature not trained for war or naturally fearless or aggressive, flee in panic at top speed for 4-24 turns.
  2. Creatures with fewer than 3 hit dice must save versus magic or be paralyzed with fear (50%) or flee in panic as above (50%).
  3. Creatures with 3 or more hit dice fight at −1 on their hit dice unless they also save versus magic.
  4. Creatures with 6 or more hit dice automatically ignore the aura.
  5. The aura of adult, old, and very old dragons is weaker than an ancient dragon’s, so saves against it are at +5, +3, and +1 respectively. For example, a 2nd-level fighter, who normally needs 16 (75%) or better to save against magic (here, the aura), gets +5 against an adult dragon’s aura, so any roll of 11 or more saves him from panic.

Speech and spells: many dragons speak one or more human languages besides their own, and a fair number of those can cast spells. Each species entry gives the chances for these, and the chance of a dragon being asleep.

Sleeping dragons: a sleeping dragon is found only in its lair. It always wakes on hearing loud noise (talking, shouting, forcing a door, etc.) within 30’ to 120’, depending on what muffles the sound (walls, doors, etc.) and how loud it is. It wakes if attacked, and also on a 6 on d6. Attackers get +3 to strike a sleeping dragon, but lose the bonus as soon as it wakes.

Some attacks work better or worse against certain dragons; the number below is added to or subtracted from both the chance to hit and the damage done.

Dragon’s breathAir*Earth**Fire***Water****Electricity
Cold0−1+1−1+1
Acid0+10+10
Gas+1000
Electricity00+1−1−1
Fire−1+1−1+10

* Includes attacks by aerial servant, air elemental, djinni, invisible stalker, or “whirlwind”. ** Earth elemental, xorn, or umber hulk. *** Efreet, fire elemental, or salamander. **** Triton or water elemental.

Dragon attacks: claw/bite or breath weapon. The breath can be used at most three times per day. When there is a choice, roll percentile dice; over 50% means the dragon breathes. The breath does damage equal to the dragon’s hit points to every creature it hits (half if a saving throw is made). Cone-shaped breath is ½” across where it starts.

  • All damage scored counts as non-fatal battering and bruising.
  • At the end of each melee round, divide the total subduing damage so far by the dragon’s hit points and turn it into a percentage (0%, 1%, 35%, 99%, or whatever). Roll percentile dice; a roll equal to or under it means the dragon is subdued. It is always subdued once the subduing damage equals or exceeds its hit points (100% or more).
  • At most one human-sized attacker per 3 linear feet of exposed dragon (not counting the tail) can attack. A fully exposed dragon with a 15’ body allows at most 11 humans (5 on each flank and one at its head).

Example of subduing a dragon: two 8th-level fighters, a 7th-level dwarven fighter, an elven 4th-level fighter/6th-level magic-user, and a 9th-level halfling thief stumble on a huge red dragon asleep on a veritable mountain of treasure. After a hurried, whispered debate they decide to subdue it, since that will a) give them a dragon to use or sell, b) save the treasure from being destroyed in a general melee, and c) make the subdued dragon point out and help carry off the best treasure. The smaller, quiet party members circle the dragon; no one stands at its head. With a shout they strike, at +3 to hit. All hit, and the halfling thief gets quadruple damage for striking from behind! They score 44 hit points of subduing damage. Being ancient, the dragon has 8 hit points per die, and being huge it has 11 dice, for 88 hit points. The referee rolls percentile dice, needing 1% to 50%, and rolls 61%.

The dragon chooses to breathe (rolling 99%), turning its head and firing right where the elf, dwarf, and halfling are attacking. After saving throws they take 44, 88, and 44 hit points of damage; all three char and die. The referee works out 67 over 88, a 76% chance of subdual, but rolls 92. The dragon fights on.

On the other hand, even a very young dragon, with only 1 hit point per die, saves according to its actual number of hit dice, for the same reason.

White dragons prefer chilly or cold regions, lairing in icy caves or deep underground places. They are less intelligent than most dragons, but as evil and greedy as any.

system.description:
A weird cross between a brass dragon and a giant lion, the dragonne is very rare and very solitary. It speaks the languages of brass dragons and sphinxes. Its small wings let it fly only short distances (1-3 turns).

  • Attacks: huge claws and great fangs.
  • Roar: its most dreaded weapon. Everyone within 12” must save against paralyzation or suffer weakness, losing 50% of their strength. Every creature within 3” is also deafened: it cannot hear any sound and strikes at −1 on its attack rolls from disorientation. Both effects last 2-12 melee rounds.

Perhaps the most feared of water creatures, found in very large rivers and lakes as well as the sea. It speaks its own tongue.

  • Defense and attacks: its thick shell makes it nearly impossible to harm, and its powerful claws and jaws easily rip opponents to shreds.
  • Steam: worse, it can belch a cloud of scalding steam 6” long, 4” wide, and 4” high, doing damage equal to its hit points, halved if the victim saves.
  • Size and age: dragon turtles vary in size, age, and hit points per die just as dragons do.
  • Ships: one that surfaces under a ship is likely to capsize it, even a large one: 95% for a small ship down to 50% for a large one.

Description: a deep green shell with silver highlights; lighter green legs and tail with golden highlights; a green/gold neck with golden highlights; and a green/gold head and crest.
system.hpNote: Size (d8: 1-2 small, 3-7 average, 8 huge) sets the hit dice; age (d8) sets the hit points per die (MM p.29). Dragon turtles vary in size, age and hit points per die just as dragons do (MM p.35).

system.description:
These beautiful, alluring tree sprites live only in the most secluded places, always near oak trees, and never more than 36” from their own tree, of which they are actually a part. Dryad trees stand out only by their large size; they give off no magic. A dryad knows the wood or forest she lives in exactly.

  • Nature: shy and non-violent. Unless surprised, a dryad can vanish by stepping into a tree, slipping out on the side the intruders cannot see, and dimension door to her own tree.
  • Charm: if seriously threatened, or near a male with 16 or more charisma, she uses her powerful charm person, up to three times per day and once per melee round, with −3 on the victim’s saving throw. A person taken away by a dryad has a 50% chance of never returning, and one who does return comes back 1-4 years later.
  • Languages: her own tongue, elven, pixieish, and sprite, and she can speak with plants.
  • Carefully approached, a dryad might be persuaded to help a person or party.

* Possible in unusual characters.

Dwarves favor rocky hills. They usually band together in clans that are competitive, though not exclusive or hostile toward one another. They can work in two or more classes at once (fighter/clerics, for example), and their level may differ in each.

Leaders:

  • For every 40 dwarves, a fighter of 2nd through 6th level (roll d6: 1 means 2nd, other numbers give the level).
  • 160 or more: also a 6th-level fighter as chief and a 4th-level fighter as lieutenant.
  • 200 or more: also a fighter/cleric of 3rd to 6th level as a fighter and 4th to 7th level as a cleric.
  • 320 or more: also an 8th-level fighter, a 7th-level fighter, a 6th-level fighter/7th-level cleric, and two 4th-level fighter/clerics.
  • Lair (always an underground complex in solid rock): also 2-12 fighters of 2nd to 5th level, 2-8 fighter/clerics of 2nd to 4th level (in each class), and females and young equal to 50% and 25% of the number of adult males.

Arms: usually chainmail and shield, with these weapons:

Sword & light crossbow15%
Sword & pole arm10%
Sword & spear20%
Axe & heavy crossbow10%
Axe & hammer25%
Axe & mace10%
Hammer & pick10%
  • Higher-level fighters and fighter/clerics have a 10% chance per level of magic armor and/or weapons. For fighter/clerics, also check at 10% per cleric level for 1-4 extra items usable by clerics (potion, cleric scroll, ring, wand/staff/rod, miscellaneous magic).
  • All dwarves above normal level wear plate armor and shield.

Guard animals: 60% chance of tamed animals guarding the lair: 5-20 wolves (25%) or 2-8 brown bears (75%).

Combat: they hate goblins, orcs, and hobgoblins, and get +1 to hit them. Ogres, trolls, and giants fighting dwarves subtract 4 from their rolls to hit, because of the dwarves’ size and skill against these huge creatures.

Other abilities:

  • Resistant to magic and poison: they save as if 4 levels above their actual level.
  • Infravision: they see monsters in the dark at 60’.
  • Mining skill: they are good (50% to 75% likely) at detecting passages that slope up or down, sliding or shifting walls or rooms, new construction, approximate depth, and unusual stonework.
  • Languages: their own, gnome, goblin, kobold, and orc, and 75% likely the common tongue too.

Description: skin usually deep tan to light brown, with ruddy cheeks and bright eyes (almost never blue). Hair brown, black, or gray. They favor earth tones with small touches of bright color in their clothing. Though only about 4 feet tall, their stocky, muscular build makes them weigh at least 150 pounds. They live at least 350 years on average.

Mountain dwarves: like their cousins the hill dwarves above, except in size (4½’+ tall), hit dice (1 + 1), and coloring (usually lighter, with brown hair). They use fewer crossbows (20% at most) and more spears (30%). Mountain dwarves with 16 strength can reach 7th level, with 17 strength 8th level, and with 18 strength 9th level. They live 400 or more years.

Giant eagles live only where there are great bluffs, cliffs, mesas, or mountain crags to nest on.

  • Eyesight: so keen they are never surprised, except in their lair or at night.
  • Diving: diving 50 or more feet, they get +4 to hit and do double claw damage (2-12/2-12), but no beak attack.
  • Carrying: up to 2,000 gold pieces at half speed.
  • Attitude: outside the lair they usually ignore good creatures but attack evil creatures that seem threatening. They are fairly friendly toward certain dwarves and elves. In their lair they are always hostile, and if there are young (50%) or eggs, they attack any creature within 50’.
  • Nests: 1 nest per 2 giant eagles, with 1-4 young per nest. They can be tamed, and eggs sell on the open market for 500 to 800 gold pieces each.
  • Language: their own, plus a limited form of telepathy.

Ear seekers are small insect-like creatures found in wood. They live on dead cellulose, but need warm places to lay their eggs, and favor places such as ears. An ear seeker that enters a warm place always lays 9-16 tiny eggs and then crawls out to die. When the eggs hatch (4-24 hours later), the larvae eat the surrounding flesh, usually burrowing inward toward the most food and body heat, killing their host 90% of the time. A cure disease spell destroys the eggs.

All eels live in water. They are usually aggressive only when approached too closely.

Electric eels live in warm fresh water and are immune to electrical effects. They give off a jolt of electricity in a 15’ radius, once per hour (six turns): creatures within 5’ take 3-24 hit points of damage, from 5’ to 10’ 2-16, and from 10’ to 15’ 1-8. Marine kinds are said to be twice the size and do twice the damage.

Giant eels are usually of the moray type, with a nasty temper and teeth to match. Few (10%) live in fresh water.

Weed eels are masters of camouflage, looking like a patch of normal seaweed to anyone but a highly trained observer. They live in colonies, sharing food and home, in fresh or salt water, usually 25’ to 40’ deep.

  • Bite: poisonous; a creature bitten dies unless it makes a saving throw.
  • Colony: a network of small holes (six to eight inches across) all leading to several 6’-wide tunnels, which lead to a communal cave about 30’ long, 20’ wide, and 20’ high. The eels floor the cave with small stones, coins, gems, metal, etc.
  • Defense: if anything tries to enter a hole, the eel it belongs to always strikes with incredible speed. If the eels notice strange creatures entering, they leave their holes to protect the cave where the young are raised.

All eels live in water. They are usually aggressive only when approached too closely.

Electric eels live in warm fresh water and are immune to electrical effects. They give off a jolt of electricity in a 15’ radius, once per hour (six turns): creatures within 5’ take 3-24 hit points of damage, from 5’ to 10’ 2-16, and from 10’ to 15’ 1-8. Marine kinds are said to be twice the size and do twice the damage.

Giant eels are usually of the moray type, with a nasty temper and teeth to match. Few (10%) live in fresh water.

Weed eels are masters of camouflage, looking like a patch of normal seaweed to anyone but a highly trained observer. They live in colonies, sharing food and home, in fresh or salt water, usually 25’ to 40’ deep.

  • Bite: poisonous; a creature bitten dies unless it makes a saving throw.
  • Colony: a network of small holes (six to eight inches across) all leading to several 6’-wide tunnels, which lead to a communal cave about 30’ long, 20’ wide, and 20’ high. The eels floor the cave with small stones, coins, gems, metal, etc.

The efreet come from the Elemental Plane of Fire, as djinn come from the Plane of Air. They are enemies of the djinn and always attack them on sight. They can travel the material, elemental, and astral planes.

  • Service: an efreeti can be forced to serve for at most 1,001 days, or until it fulfills three wishes. They are unwilling servants and try to twist their masters’ intentions by obeying the letter of their commands.
  • Once per day each: grant up to three wishes (and go free), become invisible, assume gaseous form, detect magic, enlarge (as a 10th-level magic-user), polymorph self, create an illusion with sight and sound that lasts without concentration until magically dispelled or touched, or create a wall of fire.
  • At will: produce flame or pyrotechnics, as often as desired.
  • Fire: ordinary fire does them no harm; magical fire attacks against them are at −1 on both “to hit” and damage.
  • Carrying: up to 7,500 gold pieces weight, walking or flying, without tiring. Double weight only for a limited time: three turns walking or one turn aloft, plus one more turn of either for each 1,500 gold pieces under 15,000. After carrying excess weight, an efreeti must rest for six full turns.
  • Language: a limited form of telepathy lets them understand and speak with any intelligent creature they meet.

The fabled City of Brass, the efreet citadel, is on their home plane. An efreeti can be captured there, but tens or even hundreds of efreet might have to be faced too. Efreet are infamous for hating servitude, seeking revenge, their cruelty, and their skill at misleading. A powerful Sultan rules them, served by many kinds of nobles and officials (pashas, deys, amirs, valis, and maliks).

Air elementals move only by flying, though they can of course go slower than the speed listed.

  • Air combat: fighting in the air, they get +1 to hit and +2 on each die of damage.
  • Whirlwind: on command an air elemental can form a whirlwind: an upside-down truncated cone 2” across at the bottom and 6” across at the top, as many inches high as the elemental has hit dice (8”, 12”, or 16”). Forming or dissolving it takes one full turn. A full-strength whirlwind lasts 1 melee round, sweeps away and kills all creatures under three hit dice, and does 2-16 hit points of damage to every non-aerial creature it does not kill outright. If something overhead keeps it from reaching full height, it is only half strength.

On the elemental plane of air there are certain intelligent air elementals with special abilities beyond these, some stronger than the most powerful conjured elementals. Their queen is powerful and has certain magical abilities.

Elementals: general (MM)

Four kinds of elementals are normally met: air, earth, fire, and water. They are strong but fairly stupid beings, conjured by magic from their home planes (the elemental planes of air, earth, etc.). Each kind varies in strength and has its own traits, covered under its own heading.

The elemental planes hold elementals both more and less powerful and/or intelligent than those that can be summoned. Various free-willed dwellers of those planes are described elsewhere in this book; the outstanding true elementals living there are mentioned only briefly here.

Strength: conjured elementals of every kind fall into three hit dice categories:

Conjured by spell16 hit dice
Conjured by summoning device12 hit dice
Conjured through a staff8 hit dice

Limits on conjuring: a creature can conjure an elemental only once per day per means per kind of elemental. For example, a magic-user with two suitable staffs could summon at least two elementals, one through each staff, once per day each, but not two of the same kind. If he could cast several elemental conjuring spells, each would have to summon a different kind. But if he also had a summoning device and a staff, he could possibly call up three elementals of the same kind.

Control: elementals are stupid and resent being summoned, so the conjurer must concentrate on controlling the creature.

  • Controlling it requires the conjurer to stay still and not be attacked physically or mentally, including missile attacks or distractions. Only one elemental can be controlled at a time.
  • If control fails, 75% of the time the elemental turns on the summoner, coming straight at him and attacking anything in its path. Control can never be regained, and an uncontrolled elemental always returns to its own plane three turns after control is lost.
  • If it does not turn (25% chance), it simply goes back to its own plane at once.

Harming elementals: normal weapons, and magic weapons of less than +2, do not affect them. Creatures with no magical ability of some kind cannot harm elementals unless they have four or more hit dice. Magical ability includes paralysis, poison, acid, breath weapons, and even immunity to normal weapons. So kobolds, goblins, orcs, etc. are powerless against elementals, having neither magical properties nor four or more hit dice. Ogres, though, could hurt one, having the necessary strength (four hit dice here). And a kobold with a +2 magic sword could hurt one too.

Taking over: a magic-user can take over a conjured elemental by casting dispel magic aimed at the control rather than at the elemental (chance of success: the dispeller’s level divided by the conjurer’s level). If the spell fails, the elemental is strengthened to a full 8 points per hit die, the controller’s ability to concentrate is doubled, and the elemental resents the would-be usurper, going after that magic-user if it ever becomes uncontrolled.

These powerful creatures move rather slowly. To cross water they must travel through the ground, under the bed of the water (possibly a long trip). They can be summoned from earth or stone.

  • Damage: full damage against any creature standing on the earth; −2 on each die of damage against others (flying, levitating, etc.).
  • Structures: against buildings on stone or earth they act as a super battering ram, doing 2-8 points of structural damage (a typical cottage has about 7 structural points).

On the elemental plane of earth there is said to be a boss of astounding size.

Fire elementals are terrible to behold and fierce opponents. They set fire to any flammable material they touch. Against fire-using opponents they get −1 on their damage dice. Water checks them: they cannot cross non-flammable liquids.

On the elemental plane of fire there are many different kinds of fire elementals and similar beings. The ruler of all fire elementals is said to be known as the tyrant.

  • Out of water: less effective; they lose 1 point from each die of damage they do.
  • In water: they attack at full effect and move faster. They can upset small craft (1 ton of craft per hit die of the elemental), or slow or stop vessels (1 ton stopped per hit point of the elemental; for a heavier vessel, compare tons to hit points to find how much it is slowed).

The plane of water holds many other elemental forms. Free-willed, intelligent beings are common there, as are much more powerful elementals of this kind. They may be ruled by a god-like king.

Elephants are found only in warm climates. They are fairly intelligent, fear fire, and can be trained to carry equipment and/or men.

  • Attacks: a stab with two tusks, a grab and squeeze with the trunk, and two tramplings with the front feet. No single opponent can face more than two of these attacks at once, but an elephant can fight several opponents at the same time (6 or more man-sized ones, for example). Its trunk cannot affect ogre-sized opponents, and it will not use its trunk on creatures that would hurt it (spiky, hot, etc.).
  • Gates: an elephant can easily push open a great gate unless the gate is spiked to prevent it.
  • Tusks: worth 100 to 600 gold pieces each; each gold piece of value weighs one-quarter pound.
  • Herds: if more than half the possible number is met, the herd includes 1 to 4 young, 20% to 70% grown.
  • Rogues: a single elephant is a rogue bull, with at least 6 hit points per die and a very nasty, aggressive temper. Rogues attack 90% of the time.

(See also MAMMOTH and MASTODON.)

system.treasure: Individuals N; G, S, T in lair
system.description:
There are several kinds of elves, including a marine race, all covered here. Elves can work in two or more classes at once (fighter/clerics, for example), and their level may differ in each. Their society is loose, made up of independent bands that owe allegiance to an overlord (duke, princess, king, or queen).

Leaders:

  • For every 20 elves in a band, one with above average fighting ability (2nd or 3rd level).
  • For every 40, one with that fighting ability plus 1st- or 2nd-level magic-user ability.
  • 100 or more: also a 4th-level fighter/8th-level magic-user, two 4th-level fighter/5th-level magic-users, and a 4th-level fighter/4th-level magic-user/4th-level cleric.
  • Over 160: their leaders are a 6th-level fighter/9th-level magic-user and a 6th-level fighter/6th-level magic-user/6th-level cleric, each with two special retainers (a 4th-level fighter/5th-level magic-user and a 3rd-level fighter/3rd-level magic-user/3rd-level cleric). These are in addition to the others.
  • Lair: also a 4th-level fighter/7th-level magic-user, a 4th-level fighter and a 2nd-level fighter/2nd-level magic-user/2nd-level cleric for every 40 elves, a 5th-level fighter, a 6th-level fighter, and females and young equal to 100% and 5% of the males.

Home: elves of every kind secure their homes by placing them in a secluded copse, wood, or forest, and usually (65%) have 2-12 giant eagles guarding the lair.

Arms: usually scale, ring, or chain mail, and most carry shields. A band’s weapons are:

sword and bow10%
sword and spear20%
sword20%
two-handed sword5%
spear30%
bow15%
  • Magic items: higher-level fighters, fighter/magic-users, and fighter/magic-user/clerics have a 10% chance per level per class of usable magic items. So a 4th-level fighter/5th-level magic-user/5th-level cleric has a 40% chance of magic armor (possibly including, or only, a shield) and/or a weapon (sword or other weapon); a 40% chance of any other item not covered by the first class (armor and weapons); and a 50% chance of any magic item usable by a cleric. Also, an elf above 4th level of magical ability who makes the required percentile roll has 2-5 magic items for magic-user use.
  • Elfmaids: elves do not favor horses, but rarely (5%) a band has 10-30 female fighters mounted on unicorns.

Abilities:

  • In natural surroundings such as a wood or meadow, elves move silently (surprising on 1-4) and blend into the plants so as to be invisible (only those able to see invisible objects can find them), as long as they do not attack.
  • Note their bonus with bow and sword. They are so quick and agile that they can move, fire their bows, and move back all in the same round.
  • 90% resistant to charm and sleep spells of every kind; infravision to 60’; they notice secret or hidden doors and the like one-third to one-half of the time, depending on how carefully or magically they are hidden.
  • Languages: goblin, orc, hobgoblin, and gnoll, plus common, their alignment tongue, elvish, halflingish, and gnomish.

Description: slim and pale, with dark hair and green eyes. They usually dress in pastels of blue, green, or violet (often covered by a greenish gray cloak). They live twelve centuries.

Aquatic elf: also called sea elves, they are to mermen what land elves are to men.

  • Home: almost only among heavy weed beds in quiet, sheltered salt water, where they carve caverns in lagoon bottoms and reefs to live and work. They trade with land elves: metal goods (they cannot forge underwater) for rare things from the sea.
  • Friends and foes: great friends of dolphins; for every 20 sea elves there is a 50% chance of 1-3 friendly dolphins with them. They are friends of land elves and neutral toward everyone else except fishermen, whom they dislike because so many sea elves have been caught in nets and killed in error as sahuagin by these ignorant humans. They are mortal enemies of sharks and sahuagin, and attack either if they outnumber them.
  • Arms: spears and tridents, usually with nets. They use no magic and speak only elvish.
  • Appearance: humanoid, with gill slits on the throat, greenish-silver skin, and green or blue-green hair. Seaweed hardly hinders them, and they are invisible in weeds or on reefs.

Drow: the “Black Elves” are only legend. They supposedly live deep under the surface in a strange underground realm, as dark as faeries are bright and as evil as faeries are good. Tales describe them as weak fighters but strong magic-users.

Grey elf (faerie): the rarest and most powerful of elves.

  • More intelligent than other elves (+1 on the intelligence roll); the few with supra-genius ability can become wizards.
  • Very reclusive, living in isolated meadowlands, and never mixing long or often with any humanoids but elves.
  • Usually in chain mail and shield, and all carry swords. Often (50%) they have hippogriffs as steeds (70%) or use 3-12 griffons as guards and mounts (30%).
  • They speak the same languages as high elves.
  • Either silver hair and amber eyes, or pale golden hair and violet eyes (the latter are usually called faeries). They favor white, yellow, silver, or gold clothing, often with deep blue or purple cloaks, and live beyond 1,500 years.

Half-elf: all half-elves are of human stock: handsome folk with the good features of both races, mixing freely with either.

  • Slightly taller than the average elf (5½’), weighing about 150 pounds; they live 250 years.
  • They find secret entrances and the like as elves do (one-third to one-half of the time) and have normal infravision, but do not get the elven sword and bow advantages.
  • They can advance in two or three classes at once: fighter/magic-user, or fighter/magic-user/cleric (with 13 or more wisdom). Normal maximum levels are 6/6/4; with 17 or 18 strength, fighting ability can reach 7th or 8th level; with 17 or 18 intelligence, magic-user can reach 7th or 8th level. So a half-elf can be a superhero/warlock/vicar (8/8/4).
  • Languages: the same as elves: goblin, orcish, gnoll, halflingish, gnomish, and elvish (plus alignment and common).

Wood elf: sometimes called sylvan elves; very reclusive, and usually (75%) avoid all contact. They are more neutral than other elves.

  • Unusually strong for elves (+1 on all strength rolls, treating 19 as 18), but less intelligent (treat 18 intelligence as 17).
  • Usually studded leather or ring mail (armor class 6). Fully 50% of a band have bows, only 20% carry swords, and 40% use spears.
  • Their lair is usually (70%) guarded by 2-8 giant owls (80%) or 1-6 giant lynx (20%). They live in primeval forests and distant woodlands.
  • They speak only elvish and the languages of certain woodland animals and treants.
  • Fair skin, yellow to coppery red hair, and light brown, light green, or hazel eyes. They wear russets, reds, browns, and tans, with cloaks usually green or greenish brown, and live for centuries.

system.treasure: Individual O, C, Y in lair
system.description:
Ettins are giant-like creatures living only in remote areas. They prefer darkness and are active at night, so their lairs are always underground. Their looks show they are closely related to orcs; their animal-skin clothing is usually moth-eaten and filthy, and they use spiked clubs and similar weapons.

  • Attacks: one with each arm: the left head guides the left arm (2-16 points of damage) and the right head the right arm (3-18).
  • Alertness: one head is always likely to be alert, so they are hard to surprise.

Floating eyes are very unusual saltwater fish with transparent bodies and a single large eye about three inches across, which is all that can easily be seen. A creature that looks at the eye must save versus paralyzation or be hypnotized and stay still. Predatory fish (always found near floating eyes) then eat the helpless prey, and the floating eyes feed on the scraps. They also eat any small sea creatures they come across and hypnotize.

Possibly a relative of the beholder, since the two are remarkably alike. The eye of the deep lives only at great depths in the ocean, floating slowly about and stalking prey. In temperament it is like its land-dwelling cousin, hateful and aggressive.

  • Pincers and teeth: two huge crab-like pincers to seize victims, and a mouth full of small sharp teeth.
  • Central eye: its main weapon. It gives a blinding flash in a cone (½” at the eye, extending 3” to a base 2” across) that stuns those in it for 2-8 melee rounds unless they save versus death ray/poison.
  • Small eyes: two smaller eyes on long stalks. Together they can create an illusion; separately, one casts hold person and the other hold monster.
  • Toughness: living in the deeps gives it armor class 5 everywhere, eyes and eyestalks included. It can take 10 to 12 dice of damage before dying. Severed eyestalks grow back in about a week, as a beholder’s do.

Large birds such as the ostrich, emu, and rhea, living in open grassland in warm climates. Ostrich-sized birds have 3 hit dice, emu-like birds 2, and rhea-sized birds 1. None are aggressive, and they run from danger. If cornered, they can peck (1-4 hit points) or kick (2-8 hit points).

Giant frogs live in marshes, swamps, large ponds, river banks, and lake shores. The smallest are only about 2’ long (body), medium-sized ones (2 hit dice) about 4’, and the largest some 6’. They hunt aggressively, but fear predators such as giant fish, giant turtles, giant snakes, etc. If badly wounded they retreat, and they fear fire.

  • Surprise: their coloring lets them surprise on 1-4.
  • Leaping: they can leap up to 18” to attack, and jump as high as 30’ whatever their weight. A jump can go up to 45° to either side of the way they face.
  • Weight: 50 to 250 pounds (50 pounds more for every foot of body length over 2’). For each 50 pounds over 50, subtract 2” from the 18” maximum leap.
  • Tongue: three times the frog’s body length. It strikes at +4 to hit but does no damage; it pulls prey to the mouth. A creature hit by the tongue gets a chance to hit it; if it does, the frog pulls the tongue back and does not use it on that creature again. If the tongue is not struck, the creature is drawn to the frog next turn and automatically takes maximum damage.
  • Heavier prey: a creature heavier than the frog gets a second chance to strike the tongue and is not dragged to the mouth until the third melee round. A creature more than twice the frog’s weight is not dragged at all, and the frog lets go on the third melee round.
  • Swallowing: they eat large insects, birds, rats, or almost any other creature small enough to swallow. A giant frog can swallow a small human, elf, halfling, etc. whole on a score of 20.
  • Cutting free: a swallowed victim with a sharp edged weapon can cut its way out on a score of 18 or better (this also kills the frog), with three chances to do so. Hits on a giant frog with prey inside have a one-third chance of hitting the creature inside, which then takes the damage scored on the frog.

Killer frog: these smallish giant frogs attack with talons and teeth. They are man-eating, specially bred mutants; only their cannibal habits keep them from becoming common and a real threat.

Poisonous frog: a rare variety of the normal frog. Its skin gives off a poison, so its touch as well as its bite can kill, but the poison is weak and all creatures get +4 on their saving throws.
system.hpNote: Weight is 50 pounds plus 50 per foot of body length over 2’; each 50 pounds over 50 cuts 2” from the 18” leap (MM p.41).

system.description:
Giant frogs live in marshes, swamps, large ponds, river banks, and lake shores. The smallest are only about 2’ long (body), medium-sized ones (2 hit dice) about 4’, and the largest some 6’. They hunt aggressively, but fear predators such as giant fish, giant turtles, giant snakes, etc. If badly wounded they retreat, and they fear fire.

  • Surprise: their coloring lets them surprise on 1-4.
  • Leaping: they can leap up to 18” to attack, and jump as high as 30’ whatever their weight. A jump can go up to 45° to either side of the way they face.
  • Weight: 50 to 250 pounds (50 pounds more for every foot of body length over 2’). For each 50 pounds over 50, subtract 2” from the 18” maximum leap.
  • Tongue: three times the frog’s body length. It strikes at +4 to hit but does no damage; it pulls prey to the mouth. A creature hit by the tongue gets a chance to hit it; if it does, the frog pulls the tongue back and does not use it on that creature again. If the tongue is not struck, the creature is drawn to the frog next turn and automatically takes maximum damage.
  • Heavier prey: a creature heavier than the frog gets a second chance to strike the tongue and is not dragged to the mouth until the third melee round. A creature more than twice the frog’s weight is not dragged at all, and the frog lets go on the third melee round.

Poisonous frog: a rare variety of the normal frog. Its skin gives off a poison, so its touch as well as its bite can kill, but the poison is weak and all creatures get +4 on their saving throws.

Violet fungi look like shriekers and are usually (75%) found with them. Shriekers are immune to the violet fungus’s touch, and the two help each other survive. Violet fungus prefers to grow on rotted animal matter.

  • Branches: each fungus has 1 to 4 branches that it flails at any animal within their reach. The ooze from the branches rots flesh in one melee round unless the victim saves versus poison or a cure disease is used.
  • Size: 4’ to 7’ tall. Branch length goes with size: the smallest have 1’ branches, the 5’ ones 2’ branches, etc., for a reach of 1’ to 4’. Any size can have 1 to 4 branches.

Unlike their smaller relatives, giant gar tend to be aggressive hunters. They live only in large, deep lakes and rivers.

  • Swallowing: a hit roll of 20 means the gar has swallowed its prey whole; even a small giant gar can swallow an elf or dwarf whole. A swallowed creature has a 5% chance per melee round of dying.
  • Cutting free: only a swallowed creature with a sharp-edged weapon in hand has any chance of cutting its way out, and it must do damage equal to 25% of the fish’s total hit points to get free.
  • Attacks from outside: piercing attacks on the gar can hit the swallowed creature (assume a 20% chance), doing damage to both.

Ferocious predators of a magical nature, usually found among ruins or in underground caverns. They attack anything they detect, good or evil, 90% of the time, and love best to torture helpless prey to death. Being fairly intelligent and evil, they sometimes serve an evil master of some kind.

Kopoacinth: a marine gargoyle that swims with its wings. It is like a normal gargoyle in every way, living in fairly shallow water and lairing in undersea caves.

At any distance over 10’ a gas spore is 90% likely to be mistaken for a beholder, and even close up there is a 25% chance, since it has a false central eye and rhizome growths on top that look very like a beholder’s eyestalks.

  • Explosion: if struck for even one point of damage, it explodes as its gas reacts violently with air. Every creature within a 20’ radius takes 6-36 hit points of damage (3-18 if it saves versus wands).
  • Infection: if it touches bare flesh, it shoots tiny rhizomes into the living matter, which spread through the victim’s body in one melee round, and the gas spore dies at once. The victim must get a cure disease within 24 hours or die, sprouting 2-8 gas spores.

One of the fairly common scavengers of dungeons. Its cube shape is ideal for cleaning all living things and carrion off the floors and walls of underground passages; some very large cubes are taller, to gather mosses and the like from ceilings too.

  • Hard to see: nearly transparent, so it surprises on 1-3.
  • Contents: as it travels, it sweeps up metal and other things it cannot digest, including treasure types J, K, L, M, N, Q, and items such as a potion or dagger. These stay inside it for several weeks before it casts them out on the floor somewhere.
  • Attack: a creature it touches (hits) must save versus paralyzation or be anesthetized for 5-20 melee rounds. The cube then surrounds the victim, secretes digestive fluids, and digests a meal. Its damage comes from these secretions.
  • Defenses: all weapons can hit it, and fire has normal effect. Cold has no effect unless it fails its saving throw, in which case it is slowed 50% and does only 1-4 hit points of damage. Electricity, fear, holds, paralyzation, polymorph, and sleep attacks have no effect on it.

Ghasts cannot be told apart from ghouls by looking, and are usually found only with a pack of ghouls. Powerful demons often use them as slaves.

  • Stench: once the pack attacks, their presence quickly becomes clear: they give off a carrion stench in a 10’ radius that causes retching and nausea unless a saving throw versus poison is made. Those who fail attack at −2 on “to hit” rolls.
  • Paralysis: worse, a ghast paralyzes as a ghoul does, and this works on elves too.
  • Undead: sleep and charm do not affect them. Any weapon can hit them, cold iron does double damage, and clerics can turn them.
  • Protection: a circle of protection from evil keeps them away only if used with cold iron (such as a circle of powdered iron, an iron ring, etc.).

Ghosts are the spirits of evil humans so terrible in their wickedness that they have been rewarded (or perhaps cursed) with undead status. They roam at night or in dark places, hating goodness and life and hungering to draw the life force from humans. Being non-corporeal (ethereal), they are usually met by creatures in the same state, though non-ethereal creatures can see them.

  • Sight of a ghost: its supernatural power is such that merely seeing one makes any humanoid age 10 years and flee in panic for 2-12 turns, unless it saves versus magic. Clerics above 6th level are immune, and all other humanoids above 8th level get +2 on the save.
  • Magic jar: it can attack any creature within 6” with a magic jar spell.
  • Touch: if the magic jar fails, it becomes semi-material to attack by touch, which ages the victim 10-40 years.
  • Fighting it: unless semi-material, it can be fought only by someone on the ethereal plane (where it is armor class 8) or by telepathic means. Semi-material, it is armor class 0 and can be struck only by silver weapons (doing 50% of normal damage) or magic weapons. Only creatures in an ethereal state can attack it with spells.
  • Death: any human (including dwarves, elves, gnomes, and halflings) killed by a ghost is dead forever.

Ghouls are undead creatures, once human, that feed on human and other corpses. Becoming a ghoul has deranged and destroyed their minds, but they have a terrible cunning that makes them very effective hunters. Ghoul packs always attack without fear.

  • Attacks: claws (filthy nails) and fangs.
  • Paralysis: their touch makes humans (including dwarves, gnomes, half-elves, and halflings, but not elves) go rigid unless they save versus paralyzation.
  • Spreading: any human killed by a ghoul becomes a ghoul unless blessed (or blessed and then resurrected).
  • Defenses: every attack form affects them except sleep and charm spells. Clerics can turn them. A magic circle of protection from evil keeps them completely away.

Lacedon: a marine ghoul, like ghouls in every other way.

Unlike the commoner giants, cloud giants usually live in crude castles on mountaintops or on magical cloud islands.

  • Lair: 60% likely to have 1-4 spotted lions as pets and guards. If more than 1 cloud giant is there, the second is 75% likely to be a giantess (treat as a fire giant for hit dice and damage per attack) and the rest young (roll percentile dice for how grown they are). If 6 giants are met this way, one of the young is a full-grown male, one a full-grown female, and the other two sub-adults of either sex (1-3 male, 4-6 female). Evil cloud giants have a 50% chance of 1-3 captive slaves.
  • Rocks: adults hurl rocks from 1” to 24”, doing 2-24 hit points of damage on a hit, and have a 60% chance of catching such missiles.
  • Smell: keen, so they are surprised only on a 1 on d6.
  • Clever ones: 10% are very intelligent; these are the ones living on cloud islands. They can all levitate themselves plus up to 20,000 gold pieces of extra weight twice per day.

Description: pale blue-white to light blue skin and silvery white or brass-colored hair. They wear various clothes and jewelry and are armed with great clubs.

Giants: general (MM)

Giants are huge humanoids. There are six major races, each with some similarities to the others and many differences. This section covers what they share; each race has its own entry.

  • Strength: all giants are very strong, from 19 to 24 on the human scale. This lets them pick up rocks and hurl them as if from a catapult, but without the catapult’s minimum range.
  • Homes and bags: most live in caves. Whenever they leave their lair, giants of every kind carry a huge sack holding odds and ends precious only to them: a large rock or two, and 1,000 to 6,000 coins of some kind, usually gold.
  • Nature: often stupid but usually cunning. They can sometimes be tricked, and will probably bargain if approached from a position of strength. Eager for treasure, they quite often agree to join an undertaking with creatures of similar alignment.
  • Young: a young giant’s hit points and damage are the percentage of a normal adult male’s shown by the dice roll.
  • Languages: each race speaks its own dialect, which the other races cannot understand, plus its alignment tongue.
system.hpNote: Young: roll percentile dice for how grown they are (MM p.44).

system.description:
Fire giants live in castles as often as in caverns.

  • Lair: 25% likely to have 1-4 hell hounds of the largest size as watchdogs. If more than 4 fire giants are there, the extra ones are females (as frost giants for hit dice and damage per attack), except that if 7 or 8 are met, the last one or two are young (roll percentile dice for size).
  • Rocks: adults hurl rocks from 1” to 20”, doing 2-20 hit points of damage, and catch such missiles 50% of the time.
  • Immunity: fire does not harm them, even red dragon breath.

Description: very broad (about 6’ at the shoulders), looking almost like dwarves. Coal-black skin, flaming red or bright orange hair, deep red eyes, and usually yellow-orange teeth. They wear armor or dragon hides and favor huge swords.

system.description:
Frost giants more often live in castles, though they often lair in large frigid caverns.

  • Lair: 50% likely to have 1-6 winter wolves as watchdogs. If more than 4 frost giants are there, numbers 5 and 6 are females (as stone giants for hit dice and damage per attack), and 7 and 8 are young (roll percentile dice for size).
  • Rocks: adults hurl rocks from 1” to 20”, doing 2-20 hit points of damage, and catch such missiles 40% of the time.
  • Immunity: cold does not harm them, even white dragon breath.

Description: dead white or ivory skin, blue-white or yellow hair, and pale blue or yellow eyes. Built like a muscular human, but larger. They wear armor and carry arms like those of northern barbarian humans.

system.description:
Hill giants always live in caves or similar underground dwellings, usually in forsaken areas.

  • Guards: 50% likely to have other creatures guarding the lair: 2-8 dire wolves (50%), 1-3 giant lizards (30%), or a group of 2-8 ogres (20%).
  • Lair: if more than 4 hill giants are there, numbers 5, 7, and 9 are giantesses (6 hit dice, and as ogres for damage per attack) and 6, 8, and 10 are young (roll percentile dice for size).
  • Rocks: adults hurl rocks from 1” to 20”, doing 2-16 hit points of damage, and catch such missiles 30% of the time.
  • 50% also speak ogre.

Description: tan to reddish brown skin, brown to black hair, and red-rimmed eyes. They usually dress in rough hides or skins and use any weapon available, but favor clubs.

system.description:
Stone giants usually live in mountains, in caves or caverns.

  • Lair: they are fond of cave bears, and are 75% likely to have 1-4 guarding their lair. If more than 4 stone giants are there, numbers 5 and 6 are females (as hill giants for hit dice and damage per attack) and 7 and 8 are young (roll percentile dice for size).
  • Rocks: they are playful at times, especially at night, and adults love hurling rocks from 1” to 30”, doing 3-30 hit points of damage to a creature they hit. They are 90% likely to catch such missiles thrown at them.

Description: gray to gray-brown skin, dark gray to blue-gray hair, and metallic-looking eyes (silver to steel). They are striking to look at, yet blend easily into stony surroundings, the more so because they choose rock-colored clothing. They are usually armed with stone weapons.

system.description:
The storm giant is the most powerful and respected true giant. These great, usually reclusive creatures live only in out-of-the-way places, building spacious castles on cloud islands (60%), mountain peaks (30%), or underwater (10%).

  • Animals: 30% chance of animal guards and/or pets. On cloud islands or peaks: 1 or 2 rocs (70%), which they also ride, or 1-4 griffons (30%). Underwater: 2-8 sea lions.
  • No rocks: unlike other giants, they do not hurl rocks, having magical powers and spells instead.
  • Lightning bolt: once per day, of 8 eight-sided dice.
  • Levitate: twice per day, lifting up to 30,000 gold pieces equivalent besides their own weight.
  • Water: they can breathe normally underwater when they wish. Underwater ones can still cast lightning bolts and move at normal speed.
  • Spells (one at a time, each once per day): predict weather, call lightning (3 bolts of 10-15 six-sided dice each), control winds, and weather summoning. Roused to combat, a storm giant will probably summon a storm and call lightning, the weather an angry storm giant most favors in battle.
  • Immunity: electricity does not harm them, even blue dragon breath.

Description: skin from pale light green to violet; the green shades are typical of marine storm giants. Green storm giants have dark green hair and emerald green eyes; others tend toward deep violet or blue-black hair with silvery gray or purple eyes.
