Sprites live in meadows and wooded glens. They are very shy and reclusive, but hate evil and ugliness of all kinds. They are 75% likely to go unnoticed by any creature, and attack only evil creatures unless disturbed first. They speak their own language and common.

  • Weapons: slim swords (equal to daggers) and small bows with half the range and effect of a short bow. But their arrows are coated with a special ointment: any creature struck must save versus poison or fall into a comatose sleep for 1-6 hours. The sprites then kill evil creatures, or carry good ones far from where they met the sprites.
  • Powers: invisibility at will, detect good/evil at 5” range, and silent movement. While invisible, opponents strike at −4 on “to hit” rolls.

Giant squid live in deep waters, preferring depths of half a mile or more. They are aggressive hunters and sometimes surface to attack large prey (a 10% chance of attacking a ship passing over one). They fear only the hugest sperm whales, which hunt giant squid and kill them easily.

  • Armor: a hard shell protects the body (armor class 3), but the tentacles and head are only armor class 7. If threatened, it can jet backward at great speed.
  • Tentacles: it anchors itself with two of its arms and attacks with the other 8. Each tentacle does 1-6 hit points on the first melee round it hits, then squeezes for 2-12 points per melee round. The only way to break its grip is to cut off the tentacle or kill the squid. Only one tentacle strikes a man-sized creature at a time.
  • Pinned limbs: a creature grabbed is 25% likely to have both arms pinned (cannot attack with them), 50% likely to have one pinned (attacks at −3), and 25% likely to have both free (attacks at only −1 on “to hit” rolls).
  • Severing: each tentacle takes 10 hit points to cut off, in addition to the squid’s own 12 dice.
  • Beak: bites for 5-20 hit points of damage.
  • Retreat: if 4 or more arms are cut off (or otherwise lost), it is 80% likely to squirt a cloud of black ink 6” high by 8” long, which completely blocks the vision of everyone inside, and jet backward to its lair.
  • Ships: it always tries to drag prey underwater. A seized ship is unlikely to be pulled under unless small, but the drag stops it dead in the water in 1 turn. A ship held by 8 or more tentacles takes damage as if rammed, and ships with water in their holds are easily dragged down to the squid’s lair.

Stags are plant-eaters of temperate forests and meadows: the aggressive males of a herd 4-8 times as large as the number of stags met. They defend the herd against all but the most fearsome opponents, attacking with their branching antlers or by lashing out with their sharp forehooves.

Giant stag: simply very large stags, otherwise like normal ones. A typical giant stag stands 7’ at the shoulder and weighs over 1,500 pounds.

Stags are plant-eaters of temperate forests and meadows: the aggressive males of a herd 4-8 times as large as the number of stags met. They defend the herd against all but the most fearsome opponents, attacking with their branching antlers or by lashing out with their sharp forehooves.

Giant stag: simply very large stags, otherwise like normal ones. A typical giant stag stands 7’ at the shoulder and weighs over 1,500 pounds.

Stirges are found only in very dark, tangled forests or in underground lairs. They lie in wait for warm-blooded creatures, swoop down, attach their long, sharp proboscis, and drink the victim’s blood.

  • Attack: they attack as 4 hit dice creatures rather than 1 + 1. The proboscis does 1-3 hit points of damage when it hits.
  • Draining: each melee round after it strikes, it drains blood equal to 1-4 hit points, until it has drained 12 hit points’ worth. Then, bloated, it flaps off to digest its meal.
  • The only way to detach a stirge from its prey is to kill it.

Description: rusty red to red brown feathers, yellowish eyes and feet. Its dangling proboscis is pink at the tip, fading to gray at the base.

Strangle weed is an intelligent, meat-eating kelp of fairly warm sea water. A bed of it cannot be told from normal seaweed. It grows in an oval patch of 3-12 square feet with 3-12 fronds, each 7’ to 12’ long, and attacks any creature within reach of one or more fronds. Treasure left by former victims lies beneath the sand of its bed.

  • Entwining: a hit means the frond has wrapped the victim. Each frond has 4-16 strength. The victim compares its strength with the total of the frond or fronds holding it. If the difference is in its favor, that is its chance to escape (1 = 10%, 2 = 20%, etc.). If the difference favors the weed, the victim takes that many points of crushing damage: a victim of 18 strength held by 3 fronds totaling 30 takes 12 points of damage.
  • An entwined creature strikes at −2 on its “to hit” rolls.

Su-monsters live in forsaken wilderness areas and in underground lairs. Their prehensile tails let them swing from branch to branch or hang upside down, which is one of their favorite ways of lurking for prey. Hanging this way, they can attack with all four clawed feet (all prehensile, with long, extremely sharp nails) as well as their jaws.

  • Families: if more than 4 are met, the group is likely (50%) to be a male, female, and young (for the young’s growth, roll d20 in 10% steps, treating 10% as 20% and 100% as 30%). The female fights at double value for six turns if the young are attacked, and the male at double value for four turns if the female is attacked.
  • Psionics: a latent ability lets a su-monster make one psionic attack per day if psionic activity is used within 12”. Roll d6 for the form: 1-2 psychic crush, 2-4 psionic blast (as printed), 5-6 mind thrust. It needs no psionic defense, since it cannot itself be attacked psionically.

Description: dirty gray fur, with a black tail and face and bloody red paws.

Sylphs are very beautiful creatures like nymphs, but they live mainly in the air. They love flitting about, so they are unlikely to be met near where they live. They speak their own tongue and common.

  • Friendship: sometimes (20%) a sylph befriends good creatures and helps them in some way.
  • Magic: spells at 7th level (4 1st-level, 3 2nd, 2 3rd, and 1 4th, once per day), invisibility at will, and conjure an air elemental once per week.

Thought eaters live in the ether (the ethereal plane), but their senses reach into the physical plane, and any use of psionic or psionic-related energy in either place attracts them (the range of the ability or magic is the range of attraction). To those who can see it, it looks something like a sickly gray, skeletal-bodied platypus with an enormous head, swimming through the ether with webbed paws. Only ethereal creatures can attack it. Its only desire is to feed on the mental energy of the prey it is drawn to.

  • Feeding: within 6” of any creature on the ethereal or physical planes, it absorbs any psionic or spell energy the creature tries to use. Within 1”, it can begin feeding on the actual thoughts of even non-psionic creatures.
  • Appetite: each can consume 101-200 psionic energy points before it is full. Magic converts to psionic points at 5 points per spell level, and thoughts at 10 psionic energy points per point of intelligence.
  • Intelligence loss: a creature whose thoughts are eaten loses intelligence permanently. At 0 it is dead; 1 is mindlessness, 2 idiocy, 3 imbecility, and 4 equal to a low-grade moron.
  • Protection: mental defenses, including a mind blank spell, and magic devices against psionic and psionic-related powers thwart its attacks.

Giant ticks live in forests, and sometimes in caves or caverns. They drop on prey, insert their hollow mouth tube, and suck the victim’s blood.

  • Attack: a hit does 1-4 points of damage and means the tick has attached itself. Each melee round after, it drains 1-6 hit points of blood, until it has drained as much as its own hit points; then it is full and drops off.
  • Removing it: before it is full, it must be killed, badly burned, or put under water to detach it.
  • Disease: any creature bitten has a 50% chance of catching a disease from it, fatal in 2-8 days unless cure disease is cast on the victim.

Tigers range from subarctic to tropical areas, being highly adaptable and superb hunters. They often hunt in pairs or family groups.

  • Movement: they climb well and can leap 10’ up and 30’ to 50’ ahead to attack.
  • Rake: when both forepaws hit in one melee round, they get 2 more rear claw attacks that round, each doing 2-8 hit points of damage.
  • Lair: 25% chance of 1-3 cubs, 30% to 60% grown, with no effective attacks.

Sabre-tooth tiger: the most aggressive and fearsome predator of the Pleistocene epoch, seldom met elsewhere. It ranges only in warm regions but is otherwise like a normal tiger. Its six-inch fangs cause terrible wounds, and their size together with the power of its jaws gives it +2 to hit.

  • Movement: they climb well and can leap 10’ up and 30’ to 50’ ahead to attack.
  • Rake: when both forepaws hit in one melee round, they get 2 more rear claw attacks that round, each doing 2-8 hit points of damage.
  • Lair: 25% chance of 1-3 cubs, 30% to 60% grown, with no effective attacks.

system.description:
Titans normally live on a plane somewhere above the material, but they occasionally visit the material plane for various lengths of time. Those staying on the Prime Material Plane for a long period gather treasure as shown above.

Armor class and hit dice (roll d6): 1 = armor class 2 and 17 hit dice; 2 = 1 and 18; 3 = 0 and 19; 4 = −1 and 20; 5 = −2 and 21; 6 = −3 and 22. Titans of only 17 or 18 hit dice move at 21”. Those of 21 or 22 hit dice do 8-48 hit points of damage per attack.

  • Powers: become invisible at will; levitate and/or become ethereal twice per day.
  • Spells: all titans can use both magic-user and cleric spells of 4th, 5th, 6th, or even 7th level. Roll d4 and add 3 for the number of levels of spell use in each category. Each level of spell use gives 2 spells of each category, so the minimum for any titan is 8 magic spells and 8 cleric spells: 2 of 1st level, 2 of 2nd, 2 of 3rd, and 2 of 4th. (If specific titans are not prepared, pick the spells a given titan knows at random from the spell tables when it is met.)
  • Protection from evil: a titan’s is twice normal strength against lawful evil beings.
  • Psionics: 8 or more abilities of the kinds possible for clerics: roll 2d6 and add 6 for the total (ignore levitation). Psionic strength is 100 plus a percentile roll. All abilities are used at seventh mastery level. Psionic attacks have no effect on titans.
  • Languages: their own, the six dialects of the giant races, the common tongue, and chaotic good.
  • Storm giants: titans are on very friendly terms with them, and there is a 20% chance that a storm giant is with any single titan met.

Description: titans look very much like humans, but all are very muscular and handsome, with no facial hair. Their dress and armor look Grecian.
system.hpNote: Roll d6 for armor class and hit dice: 1 = AC 2, 17 HD ... 6 = AC −3, 22 HD (MM p.94). Set the armor class to match.

system.description:
These huge, fearless plant-eaters roam the temperate plains of the Pleistocene era in herds. If more than 6 are met, 1-4 of those numbering over one-half the possible total are young, 10% to 80% grown.

  • Charge: if any creature threatens the herd, the largest animals (males) charge. A charge that strikes home does double the dice damage (4-32).
  • Trample: 2-12 per foot against any opponent low enough for them to step on.

Giant toads are found in most regions. Their smaller cousins are helpful insect eaters, but the large toads tend to devour any creature that looks edible.

  • Hop: all toads can hop their movement distance. The hop clears objects up to one-third of that distance in height and takes a single melee round, and they can attack in mid-air or at the end of the leap.

Ice toad: found in cold climates or far below the ground. Besides the usual abilities, it can radiate cold in a 1” radius from its body; every creature that does not use cold within 1” takes 3-18 points of damage. It can do this only once every other melee round. Ice toads have their own weird language.

Poisonous toad: cannot be told from non-poisonous giant toads. A victim of its bite must save versus poison or die at once.

  • Hop: all toads can hop their movement distance. The hop clears objects up to one-third of that distance in height and takes a single melee round, and they can attack in mid-air or at the end of the leap.

It can do this only once every other melee round. Ice toads have their own weird language.

Poisonous toad: cannot be told from non-poisonous giant toads. A victim of its bite must save versus poison or die at once.

Trappers are clever monsters found only in caves, caverns, and other dark places, preferring underground homes above all. They shape their flat bodies to match the floor where they lie, and with a body almost as hard as stone they are nearly impossible to detect (95%) by any normal means.

  • Attack: it usually waits until its prey is near its center (where it often makes a bump that looks like a chest or box), then suddenly closes on the unsuspecting victims.
  • Crushing: base damage of 4 plus the victim’s armor class, per turn of crushing. Those trapped cannot use weapons, since the trapper’s great muscles prevent it. Prey is smothered in 6 melee rounds regardless of the damage taken.
  • Escape: it must be killed, or faced with certain death, before it releases its prey.
  • Resistance: fire and cold do half or no damage.
  • Treasure: kept beneath it.

Description: trappers are amorphous, so they can shape themselves to the floors where they wait for prey. A typical one covers up to 400 square feet, and giant ones as much as 600 square feet. A trapper can also change its color to blend with the floor or ground it rests on.

Treants combine features of humans and trees, to which they are strangely related. They live in woods and forests and basically cannot be told from trees. They hate evil things and the unrestrained use of fire.

  • Animating trees: if need arises, a treant can make trees come to life, move 3” per turn, and attack as a full-grown treant (2 attacks for 4-24 hit points of damage each). The treant must be within 6” of a normal tree to make it move, and each treant can move only one or two normal trees this way.
  • Fire: their body and skin give them a very good armor class, but they lose this advantage against fire. Fire attacks are +4 on “to hit” dice, treants save against them at −4, and fire damage dice are +1 hit point.
  • Fortifications: treants and treant-controlled trees do 1 point of structural damage (counting both of a given treant or tree’s attacks), whatever the treant’s size.
SizeHit diceDamage per attack
Small (12’-15’ tall)7 or 82-16
Middle (16’-19’)9-103-18
Large (20’-23’+)11-124-24

Lair: typically a vast cave screened by many plants and trees. Treants greatly resent anyone entering uninvited.

system.psionicText: See below Attack/Defense Modes: See below
system.description:
Tritons are rumored to be creatures from the elemental plane of water, placed on the material plane for some purpose not yet known to man. They live in the sea, mainly in warmer waters, at shallow or great depths alike, and seldom come onto dry land.

  • Exceptional tritons: one extra of 4-6 hit dice for every 10 in a group, and one of 7-8 hit dice for every 20. A group of 50 or more is led by one of 9 hit dice.
  • Spell casters: for every 10 tritons in a group, a 10% chance of 1-4 with magical ability of 1st-6th level.
  • Mounts: 90% likely to be mounted, on hippocampi (65%) or giant sea horses (35%).

In the lair there are always these additional figures:

  • 60 males
  • 6 exceptional males of 4-6 hit dice
  • 3 exceptional males of 7-8 hit dice
  • 1 magic-user of 7th-10th level
  • 1 cleric of 8th-11th level
  • 4 clerics of 2nd-5th level
  • females equal to 100% of the males
  • young equal to 100% of the males

There is also a 75% chance of 2-12 sea lions as pets and guards. The lair is an undersea castle (80%) or a sculpted cavern (20%).

Combat: as a rule, only males fight. They wear scale armor, raising their protection to armor class 4. Mounted tritons carry long spears (lances) or tridents. The typical arms of a group:

heavy crossbow & dagger30%
sword & dagger10%
spear & dagger20%
trident & dagger40%

Conch shell horns: carried by leaders, and usually used as signals. Blown a special way, a horn calms rough waters. Blown properly, it summons 5-20 hippocampi, 5-30 giant sea horses, or 1-10 sea lions. It can also make marine creatures of animal intelligence or less flee in panic for 3-18 turns; the creatures save versus magic with −5 on their “to hit” dice rolls (as printed).

Psionics: 1 triton in 10 has a 5% chance of psionic abilities of the kind open to magic-users. If one is psionic, roll d12 for the number of abilities, chosen at random. Attack and defense modes match its potential, abilities, etc.

Languages: their own, sea elf, and locathah.

Description: silvery skin that fades into silvery blue scales on the lower limbs. Their hair is deep blue or blue-green.

History: tritons are known to serve the god Triton, and little else is known about their purpose on the material plane. They have fought fierce wars with the sahuagin and skirmish constantly with ixitxachitl, koalinths, and lacedons. They are generally friendly toward humans who mean triton society no harm.

Troglodytes are a race of reptile-men living in underground places. They loathe humans and aim to slaughter all they meet. They have excellent infravision (90’).

  • Leaders: 1 leader of 3 hit dice for every 10 met, and 2 more leaders of 4 hit dice each for every 20. If 60 or more are met, there is a chieftain of 6 hit dice and 2-8 guards of 3 hit dice each.
  • Lair: typically a large cave or cavern with small side chambers where the individual units live. It holds females equal to 100% of the males, who fight as 1 + 1 hit dice monsters, plus hatchlings and eggs, which are of no importance.

Weapons: they can attack with claws and teeth, but 50% use weapons of some kind. The armed half of a group has:

javelin (2)25%
battle axe (stone)10%
morning star (stone)10%
sword5%

Their javelins are great vaned darts, +3 to hit when thrown by troglodytes, doing 2-8 hit points of damage. They shun armor.

  • Stench: roused for battle, they give off a secretion that smells horribly to humans (dwarves, elves, gnomes, half-elves and halflings included). Those failing a saving throw versus poison are so revolted that they lose 1 point of strength per melee round for 1-6 rounds, cumulative. The loss lasts 10 melee rounds after it takes full effect.
  • Camouflage: like a chameleon, they can change their skin to shades of gray, brown, or green, so they surprise on 1-4 unless angry and giving off their stench. They use this coloring to hide when an encounter goes against them.

Trolls are horrid meat-eaters found in nearly every climate. Most creatures fear them, since a troll knows no fear and attacks without stopping. Their sense of smell is very sharp, their infravision is superior (90’), and their strength is very great.

  • Attacks: clawed forelimbs and great teeth. A troll can fight 3 different opponents at once.
  • Regeneration: beginning 3 melee rounds after it is first damaged, at 3 hit points per round, including rejoining severed parts.
  • Severed parts: these keep fighting even cut from the body: a hand can claw or strangle, the head bite, etc. Total dismemberment does not kill a troll, for the parts slither and scuttle together, rejoin, and the troll rises whole and ready to fight on.
  • Killing one: it must be burned or immersed in acid. Any separate pieces must be treated the same way, or they form a whole troll again in 3-18 melee rounds.

Description: nauseating moss green, mottled green and gray, or putrid gray hide. The writhing hair-like growth on its head is greenish black or iron gray. Its eyes are dull black.

Giant sea turtle: basically non-aggressive marine creatures, but they fight fiercely if annoyed or threatened. Surfacing under a small craft may upset it: 90% for a long boat, 10% for a typical long ship. The head and flippers are armor class 5, but can be pulled in to make these areas armor class 3.

Giant snapping turtle: greatly feared for their huge appetite and aggressiveness, found in lakes and large rivers. Being slow swimmers, they lurk near shore or on the bottom, staying still (surprising on 1-4 out of 6), then shoot out their long neck (up to 10’ long) to grab prey. The head and limbs are armor class 5, but can be pulled in for armor class 2.

Giant sea turtle: basically non-aggressive marine creatures, but they fight fiercely if annoyed or threatened. Surfacing under a small craft may upset it: 90% for a long boat, 10% for a typical long ship. The head and flippers are armor class 5, but can be pulled in to make these areas armor class 3.

Giant snapping turtle: greatly feared for their huge appetite and aggressiveness, found in lakes and large rivers. Being slow swimmers, they lurk near shore or on the bottom, staying still (surprising on 1-4 out of 6), then shoot out their long neck (up to 10’ long) to grab prey. The head and limbs are armor class 5, but can be pulled in for armor class 2.

Umber hulks are underground predators. Their iron-like claws let them burrow through solid stone at 1” per turn and through loam at fully 6 times that rate. Their prey includes young purple worms, anhkheg, and similar monsters, but their favorite prey is humans. They have their own language.

  • Attacks: claws and powerful mandibles.
  • Confusing gaze: any intelligent creature looking squarely at its four eyes must save versus magic or be confused for 3-12 melee rounds.

Description: black, shading to yellowish gray on the front. The head is gray on top and the mandibles are ivory colored. Their dark color makes them easy to mistake for some humanoid creature at 40’ or more.

Unicorns live only in temperate woodlands, away from humans. These fierce but good creatures avoid contact with all creatures except sprites, dryads, and the like. Elven and human maids of pure heart and good alignment may sometimes (25%) tame unicorns as steeds, and such unicorns are faithful, obedient mounts. Unicorns lair in open dells, keeping their guarded treasure in a nearby hollow tree, rocky niche, etc. They speak their own language.

  • Charge: a charging unicorn does not strike with its two front hooves, but its horn does double damage (2-24).
  • Horn: being magical, it is +2 on “to hit” dice. Owning a unicorn horn is a sure remedy against all forms of poison, gas included.
  • Senses and stealth: it always senses an enemy approaching within 24”. It moves very silently and surprises opponents on 1-5.
  • Dimension door: once per day it can use a short-range teleportation (a dimension door) to appear up to 36” away, even with a rider on its back.
  • Defenses: saves as an 11th-level magic-user. It is immune to poison, cannot be charmed or held by magic, and death spells do not affect it.

The night-prowling vampire is the most dreaded of the chaotic evil undead. It must rest in a coffin or similar receptacle during the hours of sunlight unless it is far below the ground, and even then it must return to such rest from time to time, since contact with soil from its grave restores its power. Like all undead, vampires exist in two planes at once, here the material and negative material. They have 18/76 strength.

  • Blow: a hit does 5-10 points of damage, and its negative force drains 2 life energy levels, with the matching losses in hit dice, ability level, attack level, etc.
  • Defenses: harmed only by magical weapons. It regenerates 3 hit points per melee round. Sleep, charm, and hold spells, poison, and paralysis do not affect it, and spells based on cold or electricity do only half damage.
  • At 0 hit points: it is not killed but forced into gaseous form. It must then return to its coffin within 12 turns, rest 8 hours, and re-form a solid body.
  • Shape changing: it can assume gaseous form at will, and shape change into a large bat whenever it wants (hence its flying movement).
  • Charming gaze: its gaze into a person’s eyes acts as charming, with the victim subtracting 2 from the saving throw versus magic. Charmed persons act as if struck by a charm person spell.
  • Summoning: it can call creatures to aid it, arriving in 2-12 melee rounds: underground, usually 10 to 100 rats or bats (the bats only confuse and block opponents’ vision, with no physical attack); in the wilderness, typically 3-18 wolves.

Warding it off: vampires recoil from strong garlic, the face of a mirror, or a cross (or several other holy symbols of lawful good) presented boldly. None of these harm it or drive it off, though. Garlic makes it hesitate 1 to 4 rounds before attacking. A mirror or holy symbol makes it move so that the object is not between it and its intended victim, or have one of its creatures remove the object holding it at bay. Lawful good holy symbols such as the cross work against vampires of every sort, whatever the vampire’s religious background in its human life.

Slaying it:

  • Sunlight: direct sunlight makes it powerless at once and kills it in 1 turn.
  • Running water: immersion kills it in 3 melee rounds; it loses one-third of its hit points per round of immersion.
  • Stake: a wooden stake through the heart kills it, but only while the stake stays in. To finish the job, its head must also be cut off and its mouth filled with holy wafers.
  • Holy water: 2-7 hit points of damage per vial that hits.

Victims: a human or humanoid drained of all life energy by a vampire becomes a vampire of suitable strength under its slayer’s control. The change takes place 1 day after burial, and only if the creature is buried. So there can be a vampire thief, cleric (chaotic evil in vampire form, of course), etc. If the slaying vampire is itself killed, the vampires it created become free-willed monsters.

Eastern vampires: invisible, with everything that implies, including −2 on “to hit” dice for opponents unable to see invisible things. They cannot charm, however, and cannot assume gaseous form at will.

Giant wasps are feared because they are always hunting prey, both to eat and to lay their eggs on in a paralyzed state. Other giant insects are their usual victims, but even humans are not safe. Some build mud cases for their eggs, but the most feared are those that build paper nests, since their lair holds 21-40 adult wasps.

  • Attacks: powerful jaws and a poisonous sting, which it can use again and again.
  • Sting: the victim must save versus poison or be paralyzed permanently, dying in 2-5 days unless a neutralize poison spell or antidote is applied. (Victims are usually eaten by the wasp larvae during those 2-5 days.)
  • Fire: their wings are very vulnerable and burn off at once within the radius of a fire ball or even when exposed to hot flame. This does not hurt the wasp but leaves it flightless.

Water weirds are a life form from the elemental plane of water. They attack all living things, feeding on their essences in some unknown way.

  • Attack: it forms from the water in two melee rounds, looking like a serpent, and lashes out, striking as a 6 hit dice monster. Any creature struck is dragged into the water unless it saves versus paralyzation.
  • Weapons: sharp weapons do only 1 hit point of damage; blunt ones do normal damage.
  • Disruption: damage equal to its total hit points disrupts it, but it re-forms in 2 melee rounds.
  • Spells: cold spells slow it, fire-based spells do half or no damage, and a purify water spell actually kills it. No other attacks harm or disrupt it.
  • Water elementals: it can take over one on a roll of 11 or better on d20.

Giant weasels are very vicious, aggressive hunters that attack until destroyed. They favor woodlands but also roam underground places when hunting.

  • Blood drain: on the melee round after a successful bite, it does not let go but sucks the victim’s blood for 2-12 hit points of damage per melee round.
  • Training: taken before half-grown and carefully trained, they can sometimes (25%) be used as hunting animals and guards.
  • Lair: always 4 or more: 2 parents and young 10% to 80% grown. The young attack too, doing damage suited to their growth.
  • Pelts: sell for 1,000 to 6,000 gold pieces.

Whales great and small (for whales) fill the oceans. Many eat plants, but a few eat meat. The meat-eaters sometimes attack humans (killer whales always do), and every kind of whale is very dangerous if bothered.

  • Attacks: meat-eating whales bite (5-20 to 15-60, depending on size). Other whales smash opponents with their great flukes (1-8 to 5-40, based on size). Whales at the surface can smash with their tails for damage equal to half their hit dice to any creature struck.
  • Swallowing: meat-eating whales swallow prey whole; the huge (36 hit dice) sperm whale can swallow a long boat and its crew whole and alive. Escape is not too hard, but digestive juices do 1 point of damage per turn, and if the whale throws up the live prey because they irritate its stomach, there is a 50% chance it does so at considerable depth.
  • Treasure: a meat-eating whale’s stomach may hold treasure: a 1% chance per hit die for each coin type, gems, jewelry, and magic items. Coins number 1,000-3,000 per type, gems and jewelry 1-20 each, and magic items 1-4.
  • Value: sick whales give off ambergris, a stinking mess worth 1,000 to 20,000 gold pieces in a large city. A whale carcass sells in a port for 100 gold pieces per hit die of size.
system.hpNote: Hit dice depend on the kind of whale; the huge sperm whale has 36 (MM p.100).

system.specialDefenses: Silver or magic weapons to hit
system.description:
The word wight has lost its old meaning of a person and now stands for the undead humans who usually haunt barrow mounds or catacombs. They are most evil and hateful, seeking to destroy any life they meet. They shun bright light and hate sunlight.

  • Weapons against them: since they exist on the normal and negative planes of the material plane at once, only silver or magical weapons affect them.
  • Energy drain: each hit does 1-4 hit points of damage and drains one experience level with all the bonuses of that level (hit dice, class bonuses, thief abilities, spell levels, etc.). A 9th-level magic-user struck by a wight loses 1-4 hit points and becomes an 8th-level magic-user, with the spells and hit points of one, and melees as an 8th-level character of his class.
  • Immunities: sleep, charm, hold, and cold-based spells, poison, and paralyzation.
  • Holy water: 2-8 hit points of damage per vial that hits.
  • Raise dead: destroys a wight.
  • Victims: a human totally drained of life energy by a wight becomes a half-strength wight under its slayer’s control.

Will-o-wisps usually haunt deserted, dangerous places such as bogs, fens, swamps, or catacombs, where mires, quicksand, pit traps, and the like are plentiful. A victim caught by these hazards feeds the will-o-wisp as it dies, for the thing feeds on the fleeing life force, so will-o-wisps try to lure prey to its doom. 10% of the time 1-3 are met, and then their lair is nearby 90% of the time.

  • Attack: it can attack; each hit does 2-16 points of electrical damage.
  • Glow: it can grow bright or very dim to confuse prey, and can move slowly or flit about. If it does not attack, it can blank out its glow entirely for 2-8 melee rounds, and then only creatures able to see invisible objects can detect it.
  • Defenses: any weapon harms it, but most spells do not. Only protection from evil, magic missile, and maze affect it.
  • Surrender: brought to 5 or fewer hit points, it reveals its lair and hands over its treasure.

Description: a glowing sphere that looks like a lantern, torch, or even a dancing lights spell effect. In combat they glow blue, violet, or pale green.

Wind walkers are creatures from the elemental plane of air. On the material plane they prefer to live high in mountains or in great caverns very far below the surface.

  • Approach: heard at 10”-30” as a whistling, howling, or roaring, depending on how many are coming.
  • Telepathy: they are telepathic and can detect thoughts within 10”-30” (working in series to boost range).
  • Attack: by wind force; each wind walker does 3-18 points of damage per turn to all creatures within 1” of it that are hit.
  • Who can fight them: being ethereal, they can be fought only by creatures such as djinn, efreet, invisible stalkers, or aerial servants, and by telepathy attacks.
  • Spells: control weather kills one unless it saves versus magic; slow affects it like a fire ball; ice storm drives them away for 1-4 melee rounds. Haste does one-half damage to them but also doubles the damage they do.
  • Pursuit: magical barriers stop them; otherwise they pursue for a minimum of 2-5 melee rounds.
  • Servitude: storm giants sometimes force them to serve (for obvious reasons).

Wolf: meat-eaters of wild forests from the arctic to the temperate zones. They always hunt in packs, and if hungry (75%) they readily follow and attack prey, always trying to strike at an unguarded moment. Their howling is 50% likely to panic plant-eating animals that are not being held and calmed by humans. They love horse meat. In the lair there is a 30% chance of 1-4 cubs per pair of adults; cubs do not fight and can be trained as war dogs or hunting beasts.

Dire wolf: simply a huge wolf typical of the Pleistocene Epoch, otherwise like normal wolves.

Worgs: evil-natured neo-dire wolves. They have a language and often work with goblins to gain prey or simply for the joy of killing. They are as large as ponies and can be ridden, and are otherwise like wolves.

Winter wolf: a horrid meat-eater of chill regions only, of great size and foul temper. They have their own language and can also talk with worgs.

  • Attacks: savage jaws, or a howled blast of frost that coats any creature within 1” of the muzzle for 6-24 hit points of damage (half if a saving throw versus dragon breath succeeds). The frost can be used only once per 10 melee rounds.
  • Defenses: cold-based attacks do not harm them, but fire-based attacks do +1 per die of normal damage.
  • Appearance: glistening white or silvery coat, very pale blue or silvery eyes. The pelt is worth 5,000 gold pieces.

Wolverines live only in colder regions, which is lucky for mankind, for these animals are horrible: vicious, hateful, destructive meat-eaters that kill for the sheer love of ending another creature’s life. Bears and wolves respect their ferocity. Only semi-intelligent in most things, they are exceptionally intelligent in hunting and combat.

  • Combat: their speed partly accounts for their high armor class, and their ferocity gives their attacks +4 on “to hit” dice rolls.
  • Musk: it can squirt disgusting musk at any opponent behind it, equal to a skunk’s (q.v.). It also deliberately ruins food or human goods of any kind by spraying musk on them.

system.specialDefenses: Silver or magic weapons to hit
system.description:
Wraiths are undead much like wights, but they exist more strongly on the negative material plane. They are found only in dark and gloomy places, since they have no power in full sunlight.

  • Touch: its chilling touch does 1-6 hit points of damage and drains 1 life energy level per hit, just as a wight does.
  • Weapons against them: only silver weapons (half damage) or magically enchanted weapons (full damage).
  • Immunities: sleep, charm, hold, and cold-based spells, poison, and paralysis.
  • Holy water: 2-8 hit points of damage per vial that hits.
  • Raise dead: slays a wraith.
  • Victims: a human (dwarves, elves, gnomes, half-elves, or even halflings included) drained of all life energy levels becomes a half-strength wraith controlled by the wraith that drained him.

Wyverns are distant relatives of dragons and live in the same kinds of places dragons like: tangled forests, great caverns, and the like. They are rather stupid but very aggressive, and always attack.

  • Attacks: a bite (2-16) and a lash of its stinging tail at one or two opponents.
  • Sting: any creature struck must save versus poison or die. Even with a successful save, it takes 1-6 points of damage.
  • Reach: the tail is very long and mobile, easily striking over the wyvern’s back to hit an opponent in front of it.

Description: dark brown to gray, with orange or red eyes.

Xorn are a race of creatures from the elemental plane of earth. On rare occasions they stay on the material plane for a time, seeking deep underground places. They feed on certain rare minerals, which are what they seek there.

  • Surprise: their jaws are very powerful, and since a xorn blends with stone (in color, in shape, and as a physical ability), it is very likely to surprise other creatures.
  • Demanding metal: it can smell metals such as copper, silver, etc. at 20’, and is likely to demand some to snack on. If a passing creature refuses, it is 90% likely to try to take the metal by force.
  • Immunities: fire- and cold-based spells do not harm them. Electrical attacks such as lightning bolts do half or no damage, depending on the saving throw.
  • Spells: move earth flings them back 3” and stuns them for one melee round. Stone to flesh or rock to mud lowers their armor class to 8 for 1 melee round, during which they cannot attack while they adjust their molecules. Passwall does 11-20 hit points of damage.
  • Escape: if a fight goes against it, it stops fighting, adjusts its molecular structure, and passes into the nearest stone (usually the floor). This takes one melee round, after which it moves at normal speed through solid stone, earth, or similar substances. A phase door spell striking it in this state kills it.

Yeti live only in regions of icy cold, so warm-blooded mankind seldom meets them. Those unlucky enough to stumble on them seldom live to tell of it, since yeti are very fond of human flesh.

  • Attacks: two clawing strikes. If either hits with a die roll of 20, the yeti has grabbed and squeezed its opponent for 2-16 points of extra damage from the creature’s chill.
  • Frightening eyes: if the yeti surprised an opponent, the victim must save versus paralyzation or have looked into its eyes and be rigid with fright for 3 melee rounds, during which the yeti automatically strikes twice and squeezes.
  • Camouflage: nearly invisible until within 10’ to 30’ of their prey. (For each level above 1st, add 5% chance of spotting a yeti at normal distance; a 2nd-level character has a 5% chance of spotting one.)
  • Fire: being adapted to cold, they are very susceptible to fire, and heat attacks do 50% more damage.
  • Lair: 30% chance of 1-3 females, and if females are present a 15% chance of 2-5 young as well.

Description: bulky, 300+ pound creatures covered in long white fur, with pale blue or almost colorless eyes and ivory white claws and teeth.

Zombies are magically animated corpses: undead creatures under the command of the evil magic-users or clerics who animated them. They follow commands, given on the spot or in advance, of limited length and complexity (a dozen words or so). They are usually found near graveyards, in dungeons, and in similar charnel places.

  • Combat: they are slow, always striking last, but always do 1-8 hit points of damage when they hit. They always fight until destroyed, and nothing short of a cleric can turn them back.
  • Immunities: sleep, charm, hold, and cold-based spells do not affect them.
  • Holy water: 2-8 hit points of damage per vial that hits.
